html:
Words | Like Jiang

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Editor’s note: We all know that noise affects our physical and mental health. But beyond its effect on people, noise also plays an important role in business. Nobody wants to live next to a railway line, and whether you’re buying a home or booking a hotel, the acoustic environment is always something to consider. Let Dr. Jiang show us how noise gets a price tag.

1. Why we need to know the price of traffic noise

Transport projects, from building an airport down to redesigning a neighborhood street, all have some noise impact, positive or negative. When we appraise a project, we want to know what these impacts cost or gain us, so that we can weigh them against the project’s other impacts, such as journey times, travel safety and air quality, and get the best possible benefit–cost ratio for the project as a whole.

Whether a transport project is worth the money depends on many factors.

Image: drawn by the author

In other situations too, such as cost–benefit analysis of noise mitigation, calculating compensation for landowners affected by noise from a new road, or setting environmental taxes on certain transport facilities and activities, we need to know the cost of more noise, or the benefit of less.

Noise impact of Heathrow Airport in 2001.

Image: Hansell et al. (2013)

In real life, however, traffic noise is not traded directly as a commodity, so there is no market price we can simply look up. How, then, do we estimate the price of traffic noise? There are currently three mainstream approaches:

1. Revealed preference (RP)

2. Stated preference (SP)

3. The impact pathway approach (IPA) (strictly speaking, IPA should not be seen as a third method on a par with RP and SP; I’ll explain why below)

Which method is simplest and easiest to use? Which is the most reliable? What is the price of traffic noise, and how far apart are the prices the three methods produce? With these questions in mind, let’s go through the three methods one by one.

2. Revealed preference (RP)

In noise valuation, revealed preference mainly means using hedonic pricing (HP) to analyze how noise affects house prices, which in turn reflects people’s willingness to pay (WTP) for noise reduction or quiet. Simply put, you run a multiple linear regression with house price as the dependent variable and, as independent variables, environmental attributes (including noise), location and accessibility, neighborhood attributes and the structural attributes of the house.

Structure, neighborhood, location and accessibility, and environment: the four main groups of attributes that drive house prices in hedonic pricing. Image: drawn by the author

The advantage of HP is that it is based on real market behavior, and now that spatial data are relatively easy to obtain and analyze, it is also fairly painless. But HP has plenty of drawbacks. It reflects the WTP of only one group of people, home buyers. It captures only the effect of noise at home, not at work, school, parks or anywhere else. The prices it produces depend heavily on the housing market in the study area, so they don’t generalize well. And those prices may also absorb the effects of other attributes on house prices (such as accessibility and air quality), because noise is correlated with them to some degree.

Noise maps are the main data source for working out the noise exposure of homes in HP noise-valuation studies. (Image: drawn by the author; data: England strategic noise mapping Round 2, OS MasterMap)

HP studies of noise valuation are as numerous as the stars. I haven’t counted them, but at a glance most use the natural log of house price as the dependent variable, so the result expresses the percentage by which house prices rise or fall for every 1 dB change: the Noise Depreciation Index (NDI).

For example, one project I worked on, with London as the case study, found that each 1 dB reduction in road noise raised house prices by 0.08%, and each 1 dB reduction in railway noise by 0.15%. These NDIs are on the low side of normal. In the studies I’ve seen, values range from 0 to 2.22%, but overall, road and aircraft noise generally come in at 0.4%–0.65%; railway noise has been studied less, so it’s hard to generalize. Multiply the percentage by the average house price in the study area, or some other reasonably representative value, and you have an estimate of the price per decibel. I should note that different studies may use different noise indicators, such as Lden, LAeq,16h and LA10,18h. Here I simply write them all as dB.

There are lots of finer points in the analysis that I won’t go into here (because I’m not confident enough to go into them...). But there is one issue I do want to raise. Most RP studies arrive at a single, constant NDI. In reality, though, if your home is in a 50 dB noise band, your WTP to bring it down 1 dB to 49 dB will be far smaller than your WTP to go from 75 dB down to 74 dB. Partly this is because decibel values are not linearly related to perceived loudness, and annoyance is not linearly related to noise level either. And even if the relationships were linear, your WTP is shaped by supply and demand: at only 50 dB, quiet is in plentiful supply, so your WTP for quiet or noise reduction is relatively low, and vice versa. Think of the old Chinese fable of the Hanhao bird, which can’t be bothered to build a nest while the days are warm.

This problem is not easy to deal with, and few studies tackle it. One that does is a study of house prices in Birmingham in 1997. In short, it split the Birmingham housing market into several sub-markets, ran a regression for each to obtain a series of NDIs, and then fitted an NDI curve that rises with the decibel level. The results of this study were the basis for noise values in England’s earlier official appraisal guidance. After a series of temporal and spatial transfers to account for prices, incomes and other factors, England’s traffic-noise values for 2002 (£ per dB per household per year) were:

<45 dB: £0;

45–50 dB: £13.7;

50–55 dB: £26.9; …

75–80 dB: £92.8;

>80 dB: £98.

The price of a McDonald’s Big Mac in the UK over the past 20 years. So how many Big Macs is a decibel of traffic noise worth? Image: www.vouchercloud.com/

3. Stated preference (SP)

Unlike revealed preference, stated preference asks people hypothetical questions so that they state their WTP directly. In noise valuation, the two most common methods are choice experiments (CE) and contingent valuation (CV). To take a simple example, a CE gives you options to choose from: say, apartment A rents for 3,000 yuan a month with 55 dB of noise, apartment B for 2,700 yuan with 60 dB, and so on. A CV asks you directly how much you would pay for a 5 dB reduction in noise, or: would you pay 100 yuan? If not, what’s the most you would pay? And so on. CE results are analyzed with conditional logit regression, with the choice as the dependent variable and the attributes of the options, including noise and rent, as independent variables. The ratio of the noise and rent coefficients then gives an estimate of WTP. To account for the effect of age, sex and so on, you can add the respondents’ characteristics and use a mixed logit model. My knowledge of CV is extremely limited, so I won’t go into how CV results are analyzed.

Traveling between Beijing and Shanghai, would you take the high-speed train or fly? That’s a real-life choice experiment. Image: https://news.qq.com/zt2011/jinghugaotie/feijigaotie.htm

Compared with revealed preference, the main advantages of stated preference are:

1. The experimental conditions can be controlled, ensuring enough variation in the independent variables, avoiding correlation between them, and so on;

2. There is more control over who is sampled;

3. The effect of individual characteristics on WTP can be studied more precisely.

Of course, the disadvantages of stated preference, or its difficulties, are just as obvious:

1. It is hard to describe a noise-reduction scenario in a question in a way that is both accurate and easy to understand;

2. Many people feel that noise is made by others and that they shouldn’t have to pay to reduce it, so WTP = 0 is common;

3. The choice of payment vehicle, whether rent, taxes or a one-off payment, can have a large effect on the results and has to be chosen sensibly for the specific context and participants;

4. It takes huge samples, hundreds or even thousands of participants or questionnaires, which is very time-consuming and expensive. In capitalist countries where everything reeks of money, getting people to take part in an experiment or fill in a questionnaire is really, really expensive.

Let me say a bit more about how noise-reduction scenarios are described. In studies of how people perceive noise or soundscapes, we usually play audio or video to the participants, but the vast majority of CE and CV studies describe the noise scenario in words on a questionnaire (I suspect this has something to do with most researchers in the field coming from economics rather than acoustics). When describing a change in noise, these studies generally don’t state it directly in decibels, because most non-specialists have no intuitive feel for a change of so many dB; even a (pseudo-)specialist like me finds it hard to imagine accurately. Instead, they usually describe things like a change in traffic volume, noise becoming “twice as loud,” or “not being annoyed anymore.” When the WTP per decibel needs to be calculated, these non-decibel changes can all be converted into decibels. Traffic volume, for example, converts to dB very directly; “twice as loud” can be treated as a 10 dB increase; and annoyance can be converted to dB with a dose–response function. (Converting between dB and annoyance with a dose–response function in this way, and then deriving the price of noise from the price of annoyance, is essentially the same as the impact pathway approach discussed later.)

The consequences of noise becoming “twice as loud” are probably more serious than many people think, wouldn’t you say? Image: https://courses.washington.edu

As with RP studies, most SP studies arrive at a single WTP value, and the values differ widely from study to study. An earlier EU study took road-noise studies from several EU countries and converted their WTP values to a common unit, € per dB per household per year at 2001 prices. The results ranged from €2 to €99. Taking the median gave the EU’s 2001 standard value for road noise: €23.5 per dB per household per year, slightly lower than England’s value for the same period. Strictly speaking, though, this value applies only where the baseline noise level is between 55 and 65 dB, because, as mentioned above, people’s WTP varies with the baseline noise level. Some SP studies have obtained WTP values for different baseline noise levels or different degrees of annoyance, but there are few of them, perhaps partly because every extra baseline noise level multiplies the number of scenarios the experimental design has to include.

4. The impact pathway approach (IPA)

In a nutshell, a typical impact pathway approach (IPA) uses dose–response functions to translate noise levels in decibels into health effects, sleep effects and every other possible impact, and then works out the cost of each. Impacts that already have a substantial body of research or receive considerable attention include annoyance, sleep disturbance, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, cognitive impairment, hearing impairment and tinnitus, productivity, learning ability and metabolic outcomes; overall quality of life, well-being and mental health can also be counted as an impact in its own right.

Many of these impacts are interrelated or even overlap, however. Lack of sleep affects the next day’s productivity, for example, and hypertension, which shows up in physiological measurements as high blood pressure, overlaps with cardiovascular disease. England’s current national guidance uses IPA but considers only three impacts: annoyance, sleep disturbance and health effects, the last of which comprises three sub-impacts: heart attack (myocardial infarction), stroke and dementia. Let’s take annoyance in England’s current guidance as an example of how IPA turns decibels into money.

About a quarter of Europeans are exposed to road noise above 55 dB. Hypertension and cardiovascular disease caused by environmental noise are estimated to lead to around 10,000 premature deaths a year in Europe. Image: https://www.eea.europa.eu/

The basic idea of the English guidance is:

Value of annoyance = population exposed × proportion highly annoyed × disability weight × health value.

The population exposed can be obtained from noise modeling or field measurements, and the proportion highly annoyed is then calculated with a dose–response function. Studies of noise–annoyance dose–response functions are, again, as numerous as the stars. The figure below shows one very well-known set of noise–annoyance curves.

A well-known set of noise–annoyance dose–response curves, from Miedema, H.M. & Oudshoorn, C.G. (2001). Annoyance from transportation noise: relationships with exposure metrics DNL and DENL and their confidence intervals. Environ Health Perspect, 109(4): 409–416. (Image: Miedema & Oudshoorn (2001))

A quick aside: if you actually regress annoyance on noise, you’ll find that noise explains very little of the variation in annoyance, often less than 50%, because how annoyed a person gets by noise also depends heavily on their personal traits and their situation. But let’s not dwell on that here; after all, standardized quantification of this kind aims to capture the typical case for the general public. The formulas for the proportion highly annoyed used in the English guidance are as follows, taken from a 2002 EU position paper:

Road:

%HA=9.868×10−4×(Lden−42)3−1.436×10−2×(Lden−42)2+0.5118×(Lden−42)

Air:

%HA=−9.199×10−5×(Lden−42)3+3.932×10−2×(Lden−42)2+0.2939×(Lden−42)

Rail:

%HA=7.239×10−4×(Lden−42)3−7.851×10−3×(Lden−42)2+0.1695×(Lden−42)

Next, the disability weight is set at 0.02, taken from a 2011 WHO Regional Office for Europe publication on environmental noise and health. A weight of 0.02 means that being highly annoyed reduces a healthy person’s health by 2%. Finally, the health value is the value of one year in full health, set at £60,000, from a 2009 UCL report.

Using IPA, England’s current guidance still expresses noise values as £ per dB per household per year, but in great detail: every 1 dB step from 45 dB to 81 dB has its own value, and road, rail and aircraft noise each have a separate set of values. For example, road noise rising from 55 dB to 56 dB costs £51, and from 74 dB to 75 dB, £167. These are 2014 values and have to be adjusted for prices and incomes before use. Of course, perfect as this may look, the values chosen for some of the key parameters at each step of the IPA remain highly contested and uncertain. What’s more, England’s guidance currently covers only three impacts, and valuing each of them requires a huge body of research or long-running studies, such as epidemiological studies, to back it up. So IPA is anything but easy.

Finally, back to why I said at the start that IPA should not be seen as a third method on a par with RP and SP. SP and RP can in fact be seen as methods for estimating the value of noise annoyance, and annoyance is just one of the many impacts IPA covers. Nor does IPA have to follow the pattern “dB → dose–response function → price”; going straight from “dB → price,” as RP and some SP studies do, works too. On the other hand, it’s hard to claim that house prices in RP studies reflect only people’s concern about annoyance and not about sleep disturbance or other impacts; and in SP studies, whether the resulting value covers only annoyance or other impacts as well depends on how the questionnaire was designed. So I think treating RP, SP and IPA as three parallel methods is not entirely correct, but it does have some justification.

5. Summary

Basically, RP, SP and IPA each have their pros and cons, and none of them is especially reliable. Even the same method can produce widely different noise values, and arguably every noise value rests on a stack of assumptions and simplifications. So those of you with a humanities background needn’t worship these quantitative valuation methods blindly. That doesn’t mean the existing methods for valuing noise are worthless, though. Perfect methods are always explored and refined step by step; and knowing how to use the numbers these methods produce to support decisions, or how to avoid bad decisions based on them, is a skill every good decision-maker should have.

Finally, thoughtful readers who have made it this far may notice that the valuation methods and results above are mainly about noise impacts at home. What about noise at schools, hospitals, parks and so on? Unfortunately, research on noise values for such places is extremely limited; it’s hard to find reasonably reliable, generalizable values, let alone do a meta-analysis. Under England’s guidance, noise-sensitive places such as schools and hospitals cannot simply be ignored; they have to be assessed case by case, possibly with some qualitative appraisal. And noise affects not only people but other animals and plants as well. There is still a long way to go before we have a complete system for valuing noise.

About the author: Like Jiang is at the University of Leeds, working mainly on urban transport and the environment, especially noise.
